source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: text-davinci-003 (GPT-3), temperature 0, zero-shot, matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on digit matrices, letter-string and four-term verbal analogies. It fell short on far story analogies.
numbers: Digit matrices: GPT-3 vs humans (N=40) odds ratio 1.88, p=.005 (generative). Letter-string vs humans (N=57): OR 1.76, p=6.3e-5, driven by zero-generalization items. Both fall as generalisations increase (GPT-3 OR 0.51; humans 0.66).
limits: Letter-string problems may sit in training data (authors say so). Humans were undergraduates; digit matrices are not equivalent to Raven (Mitchell).
agent_relevance: Headline claim that LLMs map relations zero-shot. Treat as an upper bound on easy, familiar-format mapping, not proof of a general mapping step.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (error pattern)
finding: GPT-3 showed human-like difficulty effects: progression rules, more rules, and spatially permuted logic items were all harder. Per-problem accuracy correlated with humans, r(30)=0.39, p=.027.
numbers: Spatial permutation: humans OR 0.52 p=.0017; GPT-3 OR 0.06 p=2e-11 (much steeper). Progression: humans OR 0.41; GPT-3 OR 0.07.
limits: Same direction as humans but GPT-3 effects are far larger, so it is more fragile on re-ordered layouts. Alternative reading: training text lacks complex solved cases (Hodel and West).
agent_relevance: Order and layout of the mapped elements matter a lot. A mapping step should present both sides in a canonical aligned order.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (story analogy)
finding: On Gentner-style story analogies (higher-order causal relations), GPT-3 chose the causally matching story in near analogy but not significantly in far analogy. Humans did both. A GPT-4 spot test did better in far analogy.
numbers: Near analogy: GPT-3 p=.0039, humans t(53)=21.5. Far analogy: GPT-3 p=.065 (n.s.); humans t(53)=16.7. Overall humans beat GPT-3, OR 0.37, p=.0003. 15/54 humans were perfect. GPT-4 near-perfect near, stronger far (72 problems, ChatGPT interface).
limits: GPT-4 test was small, in a web interface, not controlled like the GPT-3 runs.
agent_relevance: This is the ACME/LISA core: cross-domain mapping by shared causal structure. Weak for GPT-3, better for GPT-4. A mapping step must be checked on far cases.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (mechanism discussion)
finding: Authors link transformer attention to analogy models: pairwise similarity as in graded-similarity mapping models, and key/value indirection as a form of variable binding (the core of LISA). No test of this link.
numbers: No numbers. Argument only.
quote: Transformer self-attention involves explicitly computing the similarity between each pair of vectors
limits: Speculation, flagged by the authors as an open question.
agent_relevance: Hybrid mapping models claim role binding is key. Prompts that name roles explicitly may help; this paper does not test it.

source: Hodel and West (2023/2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Failed generalisation of Webb: simple counterfactual letter-string variants (larger interval, synthetic shuffled alphabet) break GPT-3 while humans stay stable. Argues zero-shot is unproven because such problems are on the web.
numbers: Humans stayed consistent across modifications. GPT-3 fell sharply except on remove-redundant and sort (2 of 6 types), which need no alphabet lookup. Comprehension checks: GPT-3 mostly kept at least 30 percent of its original level.
limits: Small human sample reported in appendix; GPT-3 only. Later work (Webb 2024) shows code execution repairs most of the gap.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a mapping result on a familiar surface form. Test with a surface-changed copy (matches guardrail G3).

source: Hodel and West (2023/2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models (training-data check)
finding: Asking ChatGPT for letter-string examples produced examples, weak evidence of exposure. Authors call Webb's own check weak.
numbers: Qualitative only.
limits: Circumstantial: ChatGPT had more data than GPT-3.
agent_relevance: Contamination of classic analogy formats is likely. Use fresh, generated items when evaluating the agent.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Humans (N=136 Prolific, UK) kept accuracy across permuted alphabets; GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 dropped sharply on counterfactual letter-string problems. Error types differ from humans.
numbers: Overall accuracy: humans .753 [.734,.773] on 1,876 samples; GPT-3 .488, GPT-3.5 .350, GPT-4 .452 on 6,840 samples each. Human performance steady across n=0,2,5,10,20 permuted letters.
limits: Models mostly passed counterfactual comprehension checks for successor and predecessor, so failure is not simple misreading. Counting-index explanation (Webb 2024) not tested here.
agent_relevance: Core 2020-2026 evidence that LLM analogy partly rests on familiar content. Our mapping step needs a surface-changed check.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs (error types)
finding: Error mix differs: GPT models more often commit to an incorrect rule; humans make fewer wrong-rule errors.
numbers: Table 4 (partial): Incorrect rule: GPT-3 30.97%, GPT-4 32.67%, humans 14.67%. Completely wrong: 7.74%, 2.67%, 12.50%. Another category 5.81% / 22.00% / 38.59% (row label lost in extraction).
limits: Row labels partly lost in text extraction; use with care.
agent_relevance: Rule-level errors mean the model commits to the wrong relation. A test of the induced rule on a held-out pair would catch it.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs (prompt)
finding: Used system plus user prompt with the alphabet listed and counterfactual comprehension checks; prompt format from Hodel and West. Prompt wording was not the cause of the gap.
numbers: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 tested with same format; comprehension checks mostly high.
limits: Prompt tuning was limited.
agent_relevance: Putting the alphabet or domain definitions in context is necessary but not sufficient.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2025, PNAS Nexus; arXiv 2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Rebuttal: poor counterfactual scores come from counting letters to indices in a shuffled alphabet. GPT-4 with code execution (Assistants API, gpt-4-0125-preview) reached about human level; without code it stayed poor. It was not told to use code.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1) and N=97 (interval 2), Prolific. GPT-4 hand-scored on 60 problems per interval size (10 per transformation). Fresh alphabet gave nearly identical results; older gpt-4-1106 without code did similarly poorly regardless of cutoff.
limits: Manually scored small subset; exact accuracies are in figures, not text I read. Extend-sequence at interval 2 still lagged. One model family.
agent_relevance: Strong agent lesson: hand exact index and count steps to code. The program counts, the model finds the relation. Fits schema section 1.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2025, PNAS Nexus; arXiv 2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning in LLMs (contamination control)
finding: New alphabet and an older GPT-4 snapshot (cutoff April 2023) gave the same pattern; performance tracked code execution, not training cutoff. Authors say this is inconsistent with memorisation.
numbers: Pattern described as nearly identical across two alphabets and two engines.
limits: Figures only; numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Supports using code tools for the mechanical part of mapping.

source: Stevenson et al. (2024) Can large language models generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Letter-string analogies in Latin, Greek (near) and invented Symbol (far) alphabets. Adults and 7-9 year olds held steady across alphabets; four LLMs (Claude-3.5, Gemma-2 27B, GPT-4o, Llama-3.1 405B) degraded at each step.
numbers: Children about 42-44 (age 7-9), adults 62-68, 55 runs per LLM. Latin to Greek drop p<.001 for each model (Llama p=.012); Greek to Symbol p<.001. GPT-4o matched adults on Latin; Claude-3.5 and Gemma-2 27B did not beat children on Latin.
limits: Zero-shot, best of five prompt templates. Table values not extracted.
agent_relevance: Newer models still fail the far transfer that children manage. The near-to-far gap is the mapping weakness to design against.

source: Stevenson et al. (2024) (diagnostic task)
finding: Authors ran a next/previous-letter task to check the knowledge needed, and compared item by item. Models did best on the simplest first item and worse on later ones.
numbers: Not extracted (qualitative).
limits: Partial read of section 3.3.
agent_relevance: Check the model knows the primitive relation before blaming the mapping.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Millière, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning (J. Memory and Language 145)
finding: Novel tasks map semantic words to abstract symbol sequences (re-representation, unlikely in training data). GPT-4, Claude 3 Opus and Llama-405B matched humans in the Defaults condition. Weaker models (GPT-3, Pythia-12B, Falcon-40B) did far worse.
numbers: Humans N=194 Brown students (132 + 62). Reference match 0.1-0.95 across conditions for best LLMs. Defaults: GPT-4 p=.097, Claude 3 p=.194 vs humans (not different). Reference match rises with MMLU score.
limits: Human sample is students; model specific.
agent_relevance: Re-representation is the heart of the Copycat view of analogy. Frontier LLMs can do it on fresh stimuli.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Millière, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning (J. Memory and Language 145) (permuted pairs and random finals)
finding: LLMs drop when the example pairs are shown in permuted order; humans do not. In Random Finals humans drop about 0.5 versus Only-RHS.
numbers: Claude 3 Permuted Pairs coef -1.78 (significant); humans equal across order. Only RHS: about 0.8 for Claude 3 and humans, GPT-4 about 0.9. Incoherent left side: humans lose about 0.15.
limits: Condition names from the paper; figure data not read.
agent_relevance: Presentation-order sensitivity again. Put mapped pairs in canonical order.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Millière, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning (J. Memory and Language 145) (semantic content, numeric)
finding: Semantic Content tasks: Claude 3 matched humans in all conditions; GPT-4 failed numeric conditions (could not tie object quantity to character count); Llama-405B lower on categorial.
numbers: Humans and Claude 3 about 0.7 in one condition; GPT-4 and Llama-405B about 0.35 (GPT-4 coef -1.3669, p=.002). Claude 3 range 0.4-0.7. Llama-405B numeric dual-attribute about 0.2; categorial coef -1.3139, p=.002.
limits: Single run sets; model specific.
agent_relevance: Counting fails again (matches Webb 2024). Mapping quality differs by model, so measure the chosen model.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Millière, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning (J. Memory and Language 145) (chain of thought)
finding: Chain-of-thought prompts for Claude 3 gave weak results across several prompt variants (appendix).
numbers: Not extracted (appendix).
limits: Authors call the results weak.
agent_relevance: Plain CoT is not a sure fix for mapping; do not assume it helps.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Millière, Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning (J. Memory and Language 145) (theory)
finding: Authors argue LLM success raises the burden of proof for models that posit rich built-in structure (SME, LISA-style), but variation across task versions suggests different mechanisms, so LLMs are not yet how-actually accounts.
numbers: Qualitative.
limits: Interpretive.
agent_relevance: Do not claim the agent copies human mapping; claim it needs an external check.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting: the model writes its own relevant solved problems (and optionally a tutorial) before solving. It beat 0-shot CoT and manual few-shot CoT on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench.
numbers: Codeforces GPT-4 Acc@1: 0-shot 16%, 0-shot CoT 16%, 3-shot CoT 17%, self-generated exemplars 17%, exemplars plus knowledge 19%; Acc@10 30/29/31/32/37%. GPT-3.5-turbo-16k Acc@1 8/9/11/13/15%.
limits: Gains small on GPT-4 Acc@1. Table 1 maths numbers garbled in extraction, not quoted.
agent_relevance: A real LLM-loop use of the access part of analogy. Gains modest for strong models.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models as analogical reasoners (limits)
finding: Self-generated exemplars help only with large models. Smaller models fail to produce useful exemplars; retrieved CoT does better there. Best K was 3 to 5 exemplars.
numbers: Error review of 50 samples: 35 relevant and correct, 9 relevant but wrong solution, 6 irrelevant.
limits: Manual review of 50 only.
agent_relevance: About 30 percent of self-made analogs were not usable. Needs a code-checked use, not trust (G2).

source: Yu, He, Ying (2024, ICLR) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs
finding: Agent-loop method: the LLM proposes analogous problems, solves them, and aggregates their solutions to fix the input solution. Beat IO, CoT and ToT on shortest-path, creative writing and ALFWorld.
numbers: Creative writing coherence (GPT-4): IO 6.193, CoT 6.927, ToT 7.684, TP 7.989; user preference GPT-4: IO 7%, CoT 15%, ToT 33%, TP 45%. ALFWorld all-task success: ReAct avg 57, Reflexion 79.1, TP variants 83.68 to 94.78 (6 trials).
limits: Authors' own tasks; ToT sometimes worse than IO; 2-layer TP adds token cost for marginal gain.
agent_relevance: Closest published LLM-agent use of analogy retrieval plus transfer with measured gains. Reuses successful earlier trials, like a solved-case memory.

source: Yu, He, Ying (2024, ICLR) Thought Propagation: an analogical approach to complex reasoning with LLMs (shortest path)
finding: On 100 generated shortest-path problems TP gave the most optimal and valid paths on PaLM-2, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. ToT underperformed plain IO on GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
numbers: One table block (backend not confirmed from extraction): TP 0.65 optimal, 0.89 valid, over-length 0.12; ToT 0.22 / 0.42 / 0.82; IO 0.33 / 0.50 / 0.17.
limits: Backend label of the block not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Search-style methods can hurt; analogy reuse can help. Test each against plain.

source: Webb, Sinha, Cohen (2021) Emergent symbols through binding in external memory (ESBN)
finding: A network with key/value external memory (variable binding by indirection, as in LISA role binding) learned abstract rules from hundreds of problems and generalised to unseen entities; plain LSTM, NTM and others did not do so consistently.
numbers: ESBN at least 95% generalisation to novel entities in all four tasks (same/different, relational match-to-sample, distribution-of-three, identity rules), with as few as 2 entities for same/different; mean of 10 trained networks.
limits: Synthetic tasks. Some baselines, such as Transformer and RN, generalised on some tasks.
agent_relevance: Explicit binding is the helpful ingredient, as LISA argued. For LLMs, keep role slots explicit in a written map.

source: Altabaa, Webb, Cohen, Lafferty (2024, ICLR) Abstractors and relational cross-attention
finding: A Transformer module that carries only relations, not object features (relational bottleneck). Better sample efficiency than Transformer, CoRelNet, PrediNet and MLP on relational tasks (order, SET) and on maths tasks.
numbers: Exact accuracies not extracted; learning curves in figures. Paper states consistent, sometimes dramatic gains.
limits: Synthetic and small maths tasks; not LLM scale.
agent_relevance: Design principle: separate relations from object content. A mapping prompt could hide surface content and show relations only.

source: Webb et al. (2024) The relational bottleneck as an inductive bias for efficient abstraction
finding: Review argues connectionist and symbolic views can be reconciled by constraining networks to represent relations between inputs, not attributes. Groups ESBN, Abstractor, CoRelNet as one family.
numbers: Review; no new numbers.
limits: Position paper by authors of the reviewed models.
agent_relevance: Frames the modern descendant of LISA: learned, not hand-wired.

source: Mitchell (2021) Abstraction and analogy-making in artificial intelligence
finding: Review names ACME and LISA as hybrid symbolic-connectionist mapping systems and Copycat as an active symbol architecture. Lists Copycat limits: hand-built concept network, source and target given (no retrieval), ad hoc parameters.
numbers: Qualitative. Deep nets on Raven-like data: Wild Relation Network 63% on PGM (chance 12.5%); Hu et al. found a ResNet seeing only answer panels reached about 90% on RAVEN, a shortcut.
limits: Review, no new experiments.
agent_relevance: Benchmark shortcuts inflate analogy scores. Our evaluation must remove answer-set artefacts.

source: Mitchell (2021) Abstraction and analogy-making in artificial intelligence (Copycat design)
finding: Copycat's key idea: mapping and representation building run together, with top-down concept pressure rising as bottom-up exploration falls (concept network, workspace, codelets, temperature).
numbers: Qualitative description.
limits: Restricted letter-string domain; no learning.
agent_relevance: The mapping step may need to change the problem restatement, not only map fixed facts. Tie to the reframe state, only after a failed check (G1).

source: Moskvichev, Odouard, Mitchell (2023) The ConceptARC benchmark
finding: Concept-centred ARC analogy tasks: humans far above text-only GPT-4 (temperature 0) and above the top two Kaggle ARC programs.
numbers: 16 concept groups x 30 test inputs. Humans 0.83 to 0.97 per group. Kaggle first place 0.23 to 0.77. Kaggle second 0.03 to 0.57. GPT-4 0.03 to 0.33.
limits: Text-only GPT-4 of 2023; three guesses per input.
agent_relevance: Visual analogy gap for a text model in 2023. Later models not covered here.

source: Holyoak and Thagard (1989) ACME; Hummel and Holyoak (1997) LISA; Hofstadter and Mitchell (1994) Copycat
finding: Original model papers were not opened this session. Only Mitchell 2021 and Webb 2023 descriptions were read. Original numbers belong to angles A and B.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; no figures asserted.
agent_relevance: Use secondary descriptions only.

source: Hodel and West (2024) boundary condition: lookup-free items
finding: Counterfactual items that need no alphabet lookup (sort, remove redundant) stayed near original accuracy for GPT-3.
numbers: Only 2 of 6 problem types kept accuracy near original.
limits: Figure based.
agent_relevance: Boundary: failures sit in steps that need exact position lookup, so a program can supply them.
